# Discussion

## Outcomes

The PCA and k-means clustering results suggest that data centers are not evenly distributed across the contiguous United States. Instead, they appear to be associated with certain county characteristics, particularly population and land area. This pattern is reflected in the large difference in the average number of data centers between the two clusters: Cluster 0 averages about one data center, while Cluster 1 averages about 10. This difference is notable because the PCA model used only population, county land area, and county water area. Because Cluster 0 captures more rural county characteristics while Cluster 1 aligns more closely with urban counties, these findings challenge the common public perception that data centers are primarily built in remote, open areas. Instead, our findings suggest that data centers are more prevalent in the cluster characterized by more urban county attributes. This may partly reflect our broad definition of data centers, which likely includes smaller urban deployments in addition to larger campus-style facilities. This interpretation is consistent with research by Fang and Greenstein, summarized by Pett, which identifies two major geographic patterns: third-party centers primarily cluster in dense urban markets, where proximity to customers matters, while cloud providers tend to concentrate large facilities in lower-density regions where land, electricity, and construction costs can be lower [@Fang2025; @Pett2025].

The difference-in-differences results indicate that data center presence is associated with mixed economic outcomes rather than a uniformly positive or negative effect. Data center presence’s negative effects include declines in personal income and in certain sector-specific employment measures, particularly trade and transportation, industrial, and primary industry employment. Data center presence’s positive effects include lower unemployment, increased construction activity, and lower air pollution. Taken together, these results suggest that data centers may bring real local benefits, but these benefits must be weighed against the potential economic costs that accompany them.

The decline in $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ air pollutants is limited to the more rural Cluster 0 counties and should be interpreted cautiously. Our results do not mean that data centers themselves reduce air pollution. As noted in the background section, prior research has indicated that data centers can increase $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ and related pollutants through fossil-fuel electricity generation and diesel backup generators [@Ngata2025; @Han2024]. One possible explanation for our results is a change in local industrial activity. In the same cluster, in-county threshold crossing was also associated with lower primary-industry and industrial employment. Therefore, if more emissions-intensive activity, such as mining, contracted as data center related activity expanded, overall county-average $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ could decline. Another possibility is that the introduction of highly-energy-intensive data centers led to new electricity investment and that the incremental power supply was relatively cleaner. However, those investments can support either cleaner or fossil-fuel generation depending on the regional electricity system[@DOE2025; @Ngata2025]. We did not collect data on power generation, utility investment, or facility-level emissions directly, so these explanations remain hypotheses rather than identified effects.


## Ethics

All data come from government sources and are aggregated at the county and year level. Because of this, no personally identifiable information is used in the project, rendering no major personal privacy concerns.

Hidden variables represent a significant potential source of bias. Although we use many data sources, there may still be important underlying county characteristics that are not captured in our data. For example, demographic trends or population composition may influence both where data centers are located and the economic outcomes we measure. Because we include limited demographic information, this could introduce omitted variable bias, which may cause some of our estimated relationships to reflect unobserved differences rather than the direct effect of data centers themselves. For this reason, our project is framed around associations rather than causal claims.

Another important ethical consideration is that economic data are not just abstract numbers; they represent real effects on people’s livelihoods. For example, an increase in unemployment reflects real job loss and can have serious consequences for individuals and communities. We have tried to reflect this throughout the project by using careful language and avoiding exaggerated or dismissive interpretations of the results. Any conclusions drawn from this work should acknowledge those real-world impacts.

## Limitations & Future Work

The biggest limitation of this project is the lack of consistent publicly-available data on data centers. Many private data sources are behind substantial paywalls, while some public sources do not provide historical or time-based information, and others use definitions of data centers that are inconsistent or difficult to verify. For that reason, we used the NAICS 518 definition of data centers, which gave us a consistent, government-defined measure that is reported regularly by QCEW and makes the project easier to replicate. The tradeoff is that NAICS 518 is broader than true data centers alone, so it may include some facilities or businesses that are not actually data centers or are extremely small in scale. For example, it may capture firms that provide related computing or web-hosting services but are not operating large-scale data center infrastructure.

A second major limitation is that our spatial measures are approximations of regional spillovers rather than direct measures of the geographic areas affected by data center development. Because counties do not operate in isolation, we incorporated nearby-county information using inverse-distance-weighted estimates based on each county’s five nearest neighbors. While this approach provides a useful measure of immediate regional context, it remains a simplification and may be less accurate in areas where counties are especially large, far apart, or geographically heterogeneous.

Our nearby-data center measure involves an additional spatial assumption. We constructed a 50-mile buffer around each target county’s boundary to estimate exposure to data centers in surrounding counties. Because exact facility locations were unavailable, we assumed that data centers were evenly distributed throughout each county and weighted each county’s establishment count by the proportion of its land area overlapping the buffer. This produces an area-weighted estimate of nearby data center exposure rather than an exact count of facilities within 50 miles. The 50-mile radius was selected as a plausible intermediate regional scale, but it is still a modeling assumption, and we did not test whether results would differ under alternative buffer radii. Future work could evaluate sensitivity to smaller and larger buffers, such as 25, 75, or 100 miles, and test whether these alternatives affect the magnitude or statistical significance of estimated data center impacts.

Future work would benefit most from a public dataset that includes all of: a consistent data center definition, exact facility locations, dates of operation, and size or scale measures. That would make it possible to separate large data center campuses from smaller related facilities and would improve both treatment measurement and spatial analysis. It could also test the clustered location findings more directly by measuring counties’ exact proximity to known metropolitan centers. Future work could also expand the environmental side of the project by revisiting water use and land use impacts, which we were not able to model reliably because of data availability issues. In addition, the exploratory modern machine learning work we began with the variational autoencoder could be extended further to test whether more complex non-linear relationships exist between data centers and local economic outcomes.

We also explored a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to look for additional nonlinear relationships between data centers and the outcome variables. The model did not produce clearly interpretable results. While it was a useful exploratory approach, it did not contribute meaningfully to the core findings of the project. Future research could revisit this approach, given the right-skewed distributions across our features and the likelihood of nonlinear interactions that our DiD models cannot capture.

A critical limitation of our current CVAE is that shifting the data center condition upward causes the decoder to predict positive increases across every economic variable. This contradicts our Difference-in-Differences findings, which indicate that while certain economic indicators improve with data center presence, others decline. This divergence relates to how temporal information was encoded. The year conditioning mechanism scales year values like standard numeric inputs so large values, such as 2010, do not outweigh other scaled inputs. However, this approach limits the network's ability to learn that years are sequential, reducing its capacity to encode trends over time. While passing year-over-year change features alongside raw inputs helped, it only captured single-year changes. In future work, removing the explicit year conditioning or switching to an index-based temporal encoding could force the latent space to encode longitudinal trajectories directly, rather than overfitting to single-year macroeconomic snapshots.

The model also has limitations regarding treatment definition and spatial clustering. Conditioning only happens on the number of data centers within the target county, omitting counts in neighboring counties. Because data centers cluster geographically, this setup fails to capture spillovers when facilities in neighboring counties affect the target county. Furthermore, conditioning on log-transformed data center count bins creates a different treatment condition than the DiD models' binary threshold of moving from two or fewer data centers to three or more.

Finally, the high dimensionality of our feature set and limited interpretability leave room for improvement. Many of the input features are likely redundant, and ablation testing could remove extraneous features to make the model smaller and more efficient. To improve interpretability, future work could test adding a decision tree in parallel to the decoder network, following the supervised variational autoencoder framework used by Xue and Li [@Xue2026supervised] to extract feature importance metrics from the latent space.
